hints: Focus on what you have after the first division in 14N. Every DNA molecule is hybrid, so each one has one old 15N strand and one new 14N strand.

Remember DNA replicates semi-conservatively, so in the second division each single strand separates and acts as a template for a new 14N strand. Track what the 15N strand makes and what the 14N strand makes.
walkthrough:
**Picture the starting point**

Great start, let us get clear on the setup. You begin with all heavy DNA, both strands are $^{15}N$. After one division in $^{14}N$, you are told all DNA is hybrid.

That means each DNA molecule now has: one $^{15}N$ strand + one $^{14}N$ strand.

**Apply semi-conservative replication for division 2**

This is the key idea. In semi-conservative replication, the two strands unzip and each builds a new $^{14}N$ strand from the $^{14}N$ medium.

So from 1 hybrid: the old $^{15}N$ strand makes a new hybrid, and the old $^{14}N$ strand makes a new light ($^{14}N$ only) molecule.

**Count up and get the percentage**

Let us count for the second generation. Start with 2 hybrid molecules from generation 1, they produce 4 molecules in total.

$$2 \text{ hybrids} \rightarrow 2 \text{ hybrids} + 2 \text{ light}$$ 
Percentage hybrid = $(2/4) \times 100 = 50\%$. That is option B.

options.A: Not correct. 25% would mean only 1 in 4 is hybrid, but each original 15N strand is conserved and always produces a hybrid molecule.
options.B: Correct. After the second division you get 2 hybrid and 2 light molecules out of 4 total, so 50% is hybrid.
options.C: Not correct. 75% is too high because the 14N strands from generation 1 make only light DNA in generation 2, diluting the hybrids.
options.D: Not correct. 100% hybrid was true after the first division, but after the second division half the molecules are made entirely in 14N.
